input: In this worked example, we turn our attention to a flat stainless steel wall with a thickness of 150 mm that separates two process streams, and the quantity we are aiming to determine is the steady heat flux through the wall. The thermal conductivity of the stainless steel is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference measured across the wall is 248 K, so we have all of the information we need in order to carry out the calculation. Assuming steady, one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux is obtained by multiplying the thermal conductivity by the temperature difference and then dividing by the thickness of the wall. The thickness expressed in metres is 0.15 m, and putting the numbers into the expression gives 16 × 248 / 0.15 = 26453 W m-2, which is the answer to the problem. It is worth emphasising that this is once again a conduction-only figure. The surface (film) resistances have been left out of the estimate, and including them would reduce the flux, since the films would sit in series with the wall and would absorb part of the overall temperature difference themselves. It is also worth noting that for a metal wall this particular exclusion can matter a great deal, because the wall's own resistance is comparatively small, so a film resistance of ordinary size represents a relatively large share of the total resistance. Consequently, the value of 26453 W m-2 really needs to be read as the flux for the 150 mm stainless steel wall under the 248 K temperature difference applied across the wall itself, and not as the flux that would arise across the assembled boundary between the two process streams, which would be noticeably lower.
target: A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 248 K. The worked quantity is the steady heat flux through the wall under one-dimensional conduction. The heat flux is the conductivity multiplied by the temperature difference and divided by the thickness. With the thickness taken as 0.15 m, substitution gives 16 × 248 / 0.15 = 26453 W m-2. The figure is large because both factors that set it are large in the same direction: a high conductivity carries heat readily, and the full temperature difference is applied across the wall without sharing. The figure is a conduction-only figure. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux, since the films stand in series with the wall and take part of the overall temperature difference. For a metal wall the exclusion matters more, not less: the wall's own resistance is small, so a film resistance of ordinary size is a larger share of the total, and the flux between the two streams as they stand would fall further below the stated value, in proportion, than the same exclusion would cause in a wall of low conductivity. The stated flux of 26453 W m-2 is therefore the value for the 150 mm stainless steel wall under a 248 K difference across the wall itself. No part of it should be read as the flux of the assembled boundary between the streams, where the films take their share of the difference and the wall takes only what is left. The example also fixes the meaning of its own answer: the flux belongs to the temperature difference stated for the wall, and any other difference, shared with films or measured at another place, belongs to a different calculation with a different result and a different use.
